text: Generative AI for game development, interviews with industry professionals, four voices, one shared language. Chapter 22, interviews with industry professionals. The big idea, the principles of good AI storytelling, context, adaptability, constraints, human oversight, don't belong to games alone. They show up in finance, logistics, and academia. Four professionals, four lenses. Meet the voices, Professor Nick Brown at Northeastern building adaptive narrative agents. Raghav Kandarpah, a finance data scientist crafting compliant simulations. Shivangi Saxena at Amazon simulating fulfillment workflows. And Subha Saxena at FedEx planning for failures that may never happen. Professor Nick Brown studies narrative agents, systems that adjust how they communicate based on your behavior. "We're not just building systems that

Tell stories," he says. "We're building systems that learn how to tell stories better the more they interact with people." And his warning, unbounded generation spirals into incoherence. Constraints aren't a creative cage, they're the structure that makes improvisation possible. For game developers, Brown's lesson is concrete, decide the rules of the world before the AI starts speaking. Structured prompt templates, state-driven context, rule-based scaffolds, creativity, but never chaos. Raghav Kandarpah builds immersive compliance training for a financial firm. "Narrative is the most underused training tool in corporate environments," he says. "But every fact must be grounded. If you're training anti-money laundering, the AI can't hallucinate the rules." His mantra,

Creativity without accuracy is noise. Shivangi Saxena simulates packaging and routing at Amazon before anything hits the warehouse floor. "Generative AI lets us model situations we haven't seen before," she explains. "It's like running a thousand alternative timelines and picking the best outcome." For games, that's pre-launch stress testing of every branching quest. Subha Saxena anticipates failures across FedEx's logistics network. "Reliability engineering is about mapping possibilities," she says. What could happen, what's likely, how you'd respond. It's like a choose your own adventure for maintenance teams. Her lesson for games, prepare fallback dialogue and safe recovery paths, so unexpected player behavior never breaks immersion. Four principles emerge, set the

Boundaries early, rules make creativity sustainable. Separate fact from fiction, don't let freedom undermine truth. Test before release, use AI to explore edge cases. And plan for the improbable, prepare for paths that may never be taken, but still matter. Applied to games, Brown gives us low-constrained NPCs. Raghav gives us canon-grounded quest generators. Shivangi gives us automated play-through simulation. Shubha gives us graceful fallbacks. Four industries, one shared toolkit for building AI that enhances storytelling instead of disrupting it. The takeaway, generative AI isn't a single discipline, it's a shared language spoken differently by each field. Define your boundaries, respect your truths, test before you ship, and use AI to amplify human judgment, never

Replace it. Your turn, pick one interviewee and steal their best idea. Brown's constraints, Raghav's grounding, Shivangi's simulations, or Shubha's contingencies.
